title: The Talent Read
tagline: Reading your team's skills, gaps, and flight risk.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for Vanderbilt managers: learn to read your team's skills, spot the gaps that matter, and catch flight risk while there is still time to act.
heroLead: Most managers can name their busiest person faster than their most skilled one. Today you build a working read: skills, gaps, and who might be halfway out the door.
objectives: Inventory the skills on your team beyond current job titles
Distinguish real flight-risk signals from everyday noise
Choose one talent conversation to hold this week
missionTie: Exceptional Core Operations starts with leaders who know exactly what talent they have, one team at a time.

agenda.d: Why titles hide talent, and what an inventory actually looks like.
Signals worth acting on, noise worth ignoring.
Turn the read into a talk you hold this week.

manifesto: You cannot retain, grow, or move talent you have never seen.

sections.headline: Titles tell you the job. Not the talent.
sections.lead: Every team carries skills the org chart never picked up: an analyst who writes beautifully, a coordinator who can calm anyone down. The read starts with what each person can actually do, which is always more than the job asks.
sections.group: In pairs: name one hidden skill someone on your team has that their job never uses. One pair shares.
sections.solo: Write down one hidden skill someone on your team has that their job never uses.

card.text: For each person, ask: what do they do well that the role does not require? Answers to that question are where succession plans, stretch projects, and internal moves come from.

interaction.q: Quick check: which of these belongs in a skills inventory?

opts.why: That is the role, not the person. The inventory captures what they CAN do, which is always bigger than what the job asks.

opts.t: Skills they use anywhere, in or outside the role
opts.why: Exactly. You want the full picture, including the skills the role ignores and the ones they are building on their own time.

opts.t: Only skills you have personally observed
opts.why: Your observation is one source. Ask them; people know skills they have never had the chance to show you.

interaction.context: Think about the last person you hired. You read a resume full of skills, and then the org chart reduced them to one title. Every team on this call carries skills that came up in interviews and have never been used since. The inventory question recovers what the title erased.
interaction.discuss: Whose resume surprised you when you first read it? What did they bring that their current role never touches, and what would it take to finally use it?

deeper.title: Three sources feed one honest inventory
deeper.body: Your own observation is the weakest source, because it only samples the skills the current workload happens to exercise. Triangulate three: what you have watched them do, what colleagues borrow them for, and what they say when asked directly. The third source is where the surprises live. Most people carry a skill from a past role or a side interest nobody has asked about, and will name it the first time someone does.
steps: Pick one person on your team and write three lines, one per source: seen, borrowed, self-reported. Leave the third blank until you have actually asked them.
Reread the resume or Oracle record they were hired with. Note one skill it mentions that the role has never used.
Bring the inventory line to your next 1:1 and let them correct it; their edits are the most accurate data you will get.

sections.headline: Flight risk has a sound.
sections.lead: Gallup finds 42 percent of people who quit say their manager could have done something, and nearly half heard no question about their future in their last three months. The signals were there. This section trains your ear for them.
sections.group: Breakout pairs: which signal on your team have you been calling noise? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Name one signal on your own team you may have been calling noise.

interaction.intro: Five second calls decide whether you act early or write the farewell card. Read each situation and call it.
interaction.passMsg: You can hear the difference. A signal earns a conversation this week. Noise mostly needs patience, and a growth ask deserves an answer.
interaction.failMsg: Close. Watch for pattern changes around ownership; that is the signal. Busy-season weather passes on its own, and a growth ask is good news waiting on an answer.

items.q: Your strongest analyst, who used to fight for projects, has passed on the last three without comment.
items.why: A pattern change around ownership is the classic early signal. It costs one conversation to check and months to replace them.

items.q: A steady performer is quieter than usual during the two busiest weeks of the semester.
items.why: Same person, same pattern, heavier season. Watch it, but busy-season quiet on its own is weather, not a warning.

items.q: A coordinator asks whether the department would fund a data course that is not part of their job.
items.why: That is talent telling you where it wants to grow. Fund it or find an alternative; ignored growth asks become exit interviews.

deeper.title: Read against their baseline, not the team's
deeper.body: The common mistake is comparing a person to the rest of the team: your quietest analyst looks fine next to your loudest coordinator. Flight-risk signals only mean anything against a person's own baseline, which is why long-tenured managers miss them; the baseline drifted slowly. The fix is a small discipline: know what normal ownership looks like for each person, then notice departures from that, in either direction.
steps: Write one sentence per team member describing their normal: what they volunteer for, what they own without being asked.
Flag anyone whose last month departs from their own sentence; treat the flags as things to check, never verdicts.
For one flagged person, book a light check-in this week. The conversation is how you test the read.

sections.headline: The read earns a conversation.
sections.lead: The read starts paying off when somebody hears it. SHRM's stay interview guidance runs on five questions and one discipline: ask, listen, then act on what you heard. Build the opening and the question you would actually use.

source.label: How to conduct stay interviews: five key questions (SHRM)

interaction.intro: One person on your team deserves this talk first. Choose how you open it and what you ask.

opts.t: So, are you happy here? Any complaints?
opts.coach: A yes-or-no question about happiness gets a polite yes and nothing else. Vague openings produce vague answers.

opts.t: HR wants me to do stay interviews, so here we are.
opts.coach: Honest, but it frames the talk as compliance. The person hears a form being filled in, not a manager who noticed them.

opts.t: I have been thinking about what you are great at, and I want to make sure this role uses it.
opts.coach: Specific, personal, and about them. This opening earns real answers because it proves you were paying attention.

opts.t: Nothing planned; let the conversation flow.
opts.coach: Unstructured goodwill fades fast. Without one real question, the talk stays pleasant and changes nothing.
Better than nothing, but it puts the person on the spot and invites a rehearsed answer. Ask toward growth, not exits.

opts.t: What skill do you have that this role never uses, and what would you like to build next?
opts.coach: The inventory question, aimed forward. You hear a hidden skill and a growth want in one pass, and acting on either one keeps people.

heads.strong: A conversation that retains. They left feeling seen, and you left with a talent read you can act on.
heads.mid: A decent talk that could have been a great one. The intent was right; the questions left value on the table.
heads.weak: A box got checked. The person answered politely and told a friend later that nothing will change.

reactions.strong: Two weeks later they mention the conversation to a colleague, unprompted. The stretch project you found for their hidden skill is the reason they stopped watching job boards.
reactions.mid: The conversation was pleasant and a little forgettable. Nothing broke, and nothing moved either. The signals you noticed are still there, waiting for a sharper question.
reactions.weak: The polite yes you got was the same one every departing employee gives in their last six months. The read was right; the conversation wasted it.

deeper.title: The follow-through is the retention
deeper.body: The conversation itself retains nobody; the follow-through does. Whatever you learn creates a small debt, a stretch task to find or a course to fund. Pay it visibly within two weeks, even partially, and the person learns that talking to you moves things. Miss it, and your next stay interview earns exactly the polite yes it was designed to avoid.
steps: After the conversation, write one line: the skill or want you heard, and the smallest visible action it points to.
Take the action within two weeks: forward the course link, propose the stretch task, or update your inventory and say so.
At the following 1:1, name what you did with what they told you. Closing that loop is what makes the next conversation honest.

recap.q: What belongs in a team skills inventory?
opts: What each person can do, in role or beyond it
recap.why: The inventory captures capability, not paperwork. Hidden skills are where succession and internal mobility come from.

recap.q: Your best performer stops volunteering for projects they used to fight for. That is most likely...
opts: A flight-risk signal worth one conversation
recap.why: A pattern change around ownership is the classic early flight-risk signal, and it costs one conversation to check.

recap.q: What turns a talent read into retention?
opts: Holding the conversation it points to
recap.why: The read only changes anything when the person hears it, in a stay interview or a growth check-in held this week.

recapMsgs.high: The read is loaded. Now aim it at one real person on your team.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Reread the section that got you, then build the card.
recapMsgs.low: Take one more pass through the three sections before you commit to a card.

capstone.headline: One person. One conversation. This week.
capstone.lead: Pick the person your read points to first. Role only, never a name; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: Who gets the conversation? Role and the signal you noticed.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. senior coordinator; stopped volunteering since August

practices.name: The stay interview
practices.move: Open with what they are great at, then ask what would make the next year worth staying for.

practices.name: The growth check-in
practices.move: Ask what skill they want to build next and find one real way the team can feed it.

practices.name: The skills ask
practices.move: Ask what they can do that the role never uses, and write the answer into your team inventory.

whens.out: The conversation happens this week, on the calendar by Friday.
The conversation opens your next scheduled 1:1, first item, before status updates.
The conversation happens within two weeks, booked today so it cannot slide.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did you learn that the org chart never showed you?

closing.headline: See them clearly. Keep them longer.
closing.lead: The inventory question and the flight-risk read point at the same move, one conversation this week. The rest of the week works the theme from other angles.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Hold the conversation on your card
closing.nextBody: Run it exactly as built: the opening, the question, and one line afterward about what you learned. Bring that line to next Monday's session.
closing.brandline: Read the team. Then act on the read.

facilitator.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; October is the opening month of the See the Talent Around You theme.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the conversation on your card happen? What did you learn that the org chart never showed you? What is your next talent read?' Count of held conversations is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: The skills you can't see
s1.purpose: Install the inventory question: what can each person do beyond what the role requires.
s1.say: Most of us can describe our team's workload in detail and their skills only vaguely. That gap is what this month works on. Titles tell you the job someone was hired for; half of what they can do never shows up in the role. Think about the last resume you hired from. It was full of skills, and the org chart shrank that person to a title.
facilitate: Read the lead, then put the In the room card on screen and let the resume-to-title idea land for a beat.
Run the discussion prompt aloud and take two or three voices; this is a conversation, not a quiz. The knowledge check lives in the self-paced edition only.
Run the breakout: one hidden skill per person, 90 seconds each way.

ask.q: Whose resume surprised you when you first read it, and what did they bring that the role never touches?
expect: Usually a story about a skill mentioned at hire and never used since
Sometimes silence, which is itself the point
ask.respond: If the room goes quiet: that silence is the gap this month closes. If stories flow: notice how fast they came once someone asked.

s1.debrief: The inventory question costs nothing and most managers have never asked it. Ask it this month and see what surfaces.
s1.watchFor: Managers listing job duties instead of skills. Redirect: what could this person do that the job never asks for?
s1.transition: Skills are half the read. The other half is knowing who might leave.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for one hidden skill in chat instead.

s2.title: The flight-risk read
s2.purpose: Teach the difference between actionable flight-risk signals, ordinary noise, and growth asks.
s2.say: Gallup asked people who had just quit whether it had to happen. Forty-two percent said their manager could have done something, and nearly half said nobody raised their future with them in the final three months. The signals exist; they get read as something else. So today we practice telling a real signal from busy-season weather. None of this is surveillance, by the way. It is patterns you already see in the normal course of managing.
facilitate: Run Signal or noise? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round two, pause: ask who called it noise and why. The disagreement is the teaching.
Run the breakout on the signal they have been calling noise.

ask.q: What makes the growth ask in round three so easy to miss?
expect: It sounds like a budget question
It arrives when you are busy
It is flattering, so it feels safe to postpone
ask.respond: All true. The reframe: a growth ask is talent telling you the retention lever. Postponing it is declining it.

s2.debrief: Signals are pattern changes around ownership and growth. Noise is workload weather. When unsure, one light conversation settles it.
s2.watchFor: Anyone treating this as monitoring individuals. Frame stays on patterns you observe in the normal course of managing, never on surveillance.
s2.transition: You have the read. Now it has to earn a conversation.
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

s3.title: One conversation
s3.purpose: Convert the read into a specific conversation with a strong opening and one real question.
s3.say: A talent read that never leaves your head retains nobody. SHRM's stay interview guidance keeps the format simple, five questions and the discipline to act on the answers, but the whole thing lives or dies on how you open and what you ask. So that is what we build.
facilitate: Run Build the conversation; give the room two minutes to make both choices and run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: specific opening, forward-looking question.

ask.q: Why does the compliance framing ('HR wants me to do stay interviews') kill the conversation?
expect: It makes the talk about the process, not the person
It signals the manager would not be here otherwise
ask.respond: Right. The same questions land completely differently when the opening proves you noticed them specifically.

s3.debrief: Strong talent conversations have a shape: I noticed you, here is what I see, what do you want to build next?
s3.watchFor: Managers who want a script. Give the shape, not a script; their own words are the credibility.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you build your own card.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Time to commit. One person your read points to, role only. Pick the conversation and the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere it will nag you before Friday. Two quiet minutes, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave with a read and a conversation. Hold it this week; bring what you learned to next Monday. Tomorrow's Take-Off Tuesday shows your people the Talent Marketplace, the system side of the same picture, and Thursday's session sharpens the curiosity that makes these conversations work.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Someone names a real colleague while describing a flight risk
contingencies.then: Protect them warmly and immediately: 'Hold that. Roles, never names.' The read works on patterns, not on people's reputations in a group call.

contingencies.if: A manager says they have no time for stay interviews
contingencies.then: Do the math out loud: one conversation is 30 minutes; one backfill is four to six months. The conversation is the cheap option.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't watching for flight risk just spying on my team?
toughQuestions.a: No tools, no monitoring, no message-reading. This is about patterns you already see in the normal course of managing: who volunteers, who owns, who asks about growth. The response to a signal is a conversation, which is the opposite of surveillance.

toughQuestions.q: What if the stay interview surfaces a problem I can't fix, like pay?
toughQuestions.a: Name what you control and what you don't, honestly. In Gallup's exit research, manager attention and growth drive plenty of preventable departures, and both of those are yours. For the rest, carry it upward visibly; being advocated for retains people too.

toughQuestions.q: What do I do with the skills inventory once I have it?
toughQuestions.a: Three uses this month: match one hidden skill to one real task, feed one growth ask, and hold one conversation. Later months connect it to the Talent Marketplace and the Transfer Portal, where the inventory becomes the university's map, not just yours.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Monday, 45 minutes on reading your team. Bring nothing but a quiet thought about one person on your team you would hate to lose. You will never be asked to name them. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the conversation happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the talent conversation on your card happen? 2) What did you learn that the org chart never showed you? 3) What is your next talent read?
